Could you tell I was bored today and decided to watch a random movie on HBO Max?  This was under the crime category, and seeing as how I have the urge to watch more foreign films lately, this seems like a nice place to begin. I've wasted many hours on films before, but nothing like this.  I understand the average Letterboxd user likes this film, but I don't.  I did not have a good time with this film at all.  The minute I got a half hour into it, I noticed how nothing was really happening, despite getting a labeled a psychological thriller.  Most of the movie's first half felt like a romantic drama if anything, so it looked like a drag with nothing much happening.  Come to think of it, the majority of the movie was a drag too. Shit doesn't get down until the 1 hour mark, where I started getting hopeful the movie might turn around.  The 2nd half reminded me of a Alfred Hitchcock film, which is why I felt that way.  But just when I was getting into it, the hope faded away by the end and I got slapped in the face as a result.  It might me the biggest letdown I've ever seen in a thriller/crime movie.  Even Emilia Perez had some value, and that's saying a lot. I was thinking while writing this review how prior to this, I had the idea of watching an old MGM movie on Blu-ray, but the other side of my brain said to find a movie from HBO Max instead because they usually have a vast library of films.  Man, I should've just went for the MGM movie. The Swimming Pool may be good like some people here said.  Maybe I just didn't see it right according to them, but I feel like I saw enough to be absolutely baffled.  I don't care if anyone hates me for this opinion, because I'm already too stunned to fight back.

This is one of those films that had completely passed me by. I went in knowing absolutely nothing about it and was impressed by much of what it had to offer. There are some excellent performances, one sequence that was genuinely cold and horrific, and one of Michel Legrand’s more entertaining scores. The jazzy pop songs are so bad they’re almost good. However, at over two hours long, the film is at times mind-numbingly dull. Deray is a fine director, but I feel his love of the material has blinkered him to how much depth it really has. When, halfway through, I found myself thinking how much more entertaining this would have been if Jess Franco had directed it, I knew it wasn’t fully connecting with me. It’s interesting and definitely a film that could spark debate, provided you don’t nod off during it. I’m glad I watched it, but I can't say that I'll be returning to it anytime soon.

A phone call interrupts a poolside make-out session. A thirtysomething couple, Jean-Paul (Alain Delon) and Marianne (Romy Schneider), are vacationing at a lavish Saint-Tropez villa owned by absent friends. The phone call brings to the villa two visitors. One is an old friend of theirs and an ex-lover of Marianne's, Harry (Maurice Ronet), a pop music producer. The second visitor is his eighteen-year-old daughter, Penelope, played by Jane Birken. Birken is too physically mature to pass as a teenager, but she captures some of that age's awkwardness, its sullen remoteness. Jean-Paul has questions about the romance Marianne had with Harry, long-standing questions the visit rekindles as it also conjures versions of the selves these old friends were and futures they lost. Rivalries grow. The camera lingers over tan, fit bodies, both male and female, and eyes scoping other bodies. Legs abound, Marianne and Penelope's especially, in the first hour. The music quiets down in the second hour too. That helps. The look and looking are of its era. As is the acting. The disappointments and  transgressions are transhistorical. And pools . . . "Some nights anything goes," Jean-Paul tells Penelope. "Or almost anything." Emotional engagement slips gradually away so that the final embrace contrasts brutally with the sun-drenched eroticism of the opening scene.

There is a tension in their relationship which excites Marianne: the film begins with a scene in which they are together beside the villa's swimming pool and she urges him to scratch her back. He does as she asks, but then throws her into the pool and jumps in after her. In a later scene he takes a branch and uses it to lash her bare buttocks, playfully but with a force that increases as the scene cuts away. Harry (Ronet), an old friend and record producer who was Marianne's lover before Jean-Paul, arrives for a visit, surprising the couple by bringing along his 18-year-old daughter Penelope (Birkin), whose existence they had not previously known about. Marianne, without asking Jean-Paul, invites Harry and Penelope to stay. The four stay together and Harry draws Marianne back towards him as the days go by. Taunting Jean-Paul for having given up serious writing to work in advertising, Harry drinks a great deal and throws a surprise party while Jean-Paul, a recovering alcoholic, stays sober. Meanwhile, it becomes clear that Penelope neither likes nor respects her father, whom she has barely known while growing up. She and Jean-Paul become close and spend a day alone together by the sea. That night, while the women are asleep, Harry drunkenly confronts Jean-Paul and accuses him of seducing Penelope to revenge his own shortcomings on his more successful friend. Trying to punch Jean-Paul, Harry falls into the pool and is too drunk to swim. Jean-Paul, who has also been drinking, at first stops him from climbing out of the water, then deliberately pushes Harry under and holds him down until he drowns. He covers up the crime by stripping Harry's clothes off and placing fresh trousers and a shirt at the poolside to make it look like an accident. After the funeral, a policeman, Inspector Lévêque (Crauchet), visits the house more than once. He confides to Marianne his reasons for doubting the story of an accident, that Harry had been wearing his watch, which was expensive and not waterproof, and that there is no trace of sweat on the clothes he was supposed to have been wearing. When she tells Jean-Paul, he confesses everything to her, and she goes to see Harry's clothes, hidden in the cellar, that would have given him away. But when she does not take this evidence to the police, the inspector reluctantly suspends the inquiry. Marianne takes Penelope to the airport and sees her off as she returns to her mother. When Penelope demands the truth about her father's death, Marianne assures her it really was an accident. She and Jean-Paul are then about to leave the villa when she tells him that they will not go together. She calls for a taxi but he places his hand on the telephone, cutting off her call and silencing her. In the end, neither leaves that day, and in the film's final shot they stand side by side looking out the window at the swimming pool, and then embrace.

Summer doesn’t feel like it’s over quite yet in SoCal, so I have an excuse for squeezing this one in. The characters, being French, just had to flex the eons of PTO they use to go en vacances : “He [Jean-Paul] only has a month off.” Ma’am… ONLY?! Equally enviable is the house at which Jean-Paul and Marianne are staying, only a short drive from St. Tropez. It’s a sun-drenched, erotic idyll, and you already know Delon and Schneider came to play w/r/t their beach bodies. Delon’s character Jean-Paul is sufficiently proud of his to greet both a friend he hadn’t seen in years and the friend’s teenaged daughter (whom he’d never previously met), without so much as putting on a shirt first. As it turns out, Harry the newly arrived frenemy has a history with Marianne; meanwhile Jean-Paul and the 18-year-old Pénélope enjoy an ill-concealed spark. You don’t exactly want your old pal sleeping with your daughter (especially if you're a father portrayed with certain incestuous undertones), any more than you’d want a successful, Maserati-driving competitor cozying up to your steady girl. After Jean-Paul and Harry have their inevitable clash, the movie will take a hard left turn into an entirely different genre. La Piscine is stitched together with such a hodgepodge of jarring hard cuts and bravura feats of montage that I can’t get a good read on Mr. Deray after just one film. At one point the guys take Harry’s Maserati out for a joy ride, and with the hum of that Italian motor still sounding on the audio track, he cuts to Marianne’s nude figure lying face-down in bed, slowly panning from thigh to shoulder, so that intercutting back to the Maserati may well result in our appraising the shapely curves of that car’s body in a new light. It’s not that I have a car fetish (don't knock it till I've tried it?); I’m merely describing what Deray is showing me. Anyway, the one hard cut that worked to perfection happens just after Jean-Paul and Pénélope have made meaningful eye contact, and at that very moment a chorus of car horns begins to blare as we cut to a caravan of party guests pulling up to the house later that evening. As for the party, I was gratified to see that the two dudes who brought acoustic guitars had the decency to play them outside, a good, safe distance from the main group. Not that the main group's choice of music was any major improvement: there’s a song, "Ask Yourself Why," that plays twice in the film, and it is horrid on all fronts—melody, vocal performance, the works. Mute until next subtitle event for best experience. After the party, when the characters aren’t having fun anymore, I was feeling much the same way. During the awkward dinner of homemade Chinese, it was mildly unpleasant to hear a bunch of Euros pontificating at length on how Chinese food should properly be made. It may have been a deliberate choice, contributing to the awkwardness; I’m not certain. Whatever the case, Alain Delon was putting that shit on in the final act: the white knit sweater, the shades… he had it all working. He wears the sunglasses simply for his hangover at first, but in due course the situation calls for a top-quality poker face, and so the man goes all LaDainian Tomlinson, like when the Chargers great would wear the tinted helmet visor to keep the defenses guessing. Long story short, La Piscine may not be high art exactly, but I heartily enjoyed it, the first hour-plus in particular.

The Swimming Pool turns a seemingly idyllic summer holiday into a tense study of desire, jealousy and guilt. Jean-Paul and Marianne appear to enjoy a carefree summer at their secluded villa until Marianne invites her former lover Harry and his daughter Penelope , whose arrival brings old feelings, insecurities, and unspoken resentments to the surface. What I liked most is how the film builds tension through small shifts in behavior rather than constant dramatic confrontation. Jean-Paul becomes increasingly jealous of Harry’s confidence and Marianne’s familiarity with him while Penelope’s presence adds another layer of attraction and uneasiness to the group. The beautiful Mediterranean setting and Alain Delon and Romy Schneider’s restrained performances create an atmosphere that feels both sensual and strangely suffocating. The slow pacing and emotionally distant characters kept me from fully investing but I liked how the film blurs desire, guilt and reality through Jean-Paul’s fears.

The near-total absence of a soundtrack creates a sensation akin to a stillness—it doesn’t make the scene oppressive, but it does make it feel heavy, as if mirroring the sweltering heat. The murder is a natural consequence of the protagonists’ actions; they voluntarily decide to start teasing and annoying each other as if it were a game, but it eventually spirals out of control. The two protagonists are no longer so young and are already beginning to show their first wrinkles and imperfections. They aren’t the perfect embodiment of youth, but they don’t seem aged either. They’re in a middle ground, as if suspended in time. Both are beautiful but show the weariness that comes with more years under their belts. The most unrealistic element of the film? Superb mise-en-scène, I don't think I've ever wanted to inhabit a movie so much as this one. Imagine vacationing here for a whole month! The place, the architecture, the clothing, the music, the furniture, the food, I WANT TO BE THERE!! That aside, this would be a mediocre movie if you had to explain its paper thin plot. Where it shines, and why I think it is underrated (literally underrated here with a mere 3.7) is because of the deep characters and their complex power dynamics. You don't see their stories, you don't know their relationships, you're thrown into this group like a voyeur watching his holiday neighbors. You have to think, dissect and analyze each seen, and understand why the characters made such and such decisions and what does that say about them. Each of them has hidden agendas, each of them seem to be madly in love about the other but actually wants to use them to provoke another character. It is a delight to uncover their stories and personalities little by little, and also after finishing it, to remember their first actions and interactions and see how well made they were from the beginning and how much each line reveals something about them. Great film, and I hope to see more of Alain Delon and Jane Birking as well who I didn't know was in this film. Everyone desires something, and none of them seem to truly desire one another.

La Piscine é um daqueles filmes que vivem quase exclusivamente daquilo que fica por dizer, senti tensão no silêncio. A narrativa é simples, mas a forma como Jacques Deray manipula o espaço, o tempo e as relações entre as personagens faz com que exista uma tensão constante, mesmo quando aparentemente nada está a acontecer, e foi algo que eu adorei. É um filme que percebe que o desconforto nasce muito antes do conflito e constrói essa sensação com uma subtileza rara. O mais interessante é a maneira como o calor, a piscina e aquela casa isolada deixam de ser apenas cenário e passam a refletir o estado emocional das personagens, tudo parece demasiado confortável, demasiado perfeito, e é precisamente essa aparência de tranquilidade que torna inevitável a implosão. A mise-en-scène é extremamente rigorosa, sem nunca chamar demasiado a atenção para si própria, e isso faz com que cada olhar ou pausa tenha um peso desproporcional. Maurice Ronet introduz uma presença que desestabiliza toda a dinâmica do grupo, eu gosto que não exista propriamente heróis nem vilões, há egos, inseguranças e um desejo constante de validação que acaba por contaminar todas as relações. O filme evita julgamentos morais fáceis e acredito que prefira explorar as ambiguidades que surgem quando o desejo, o ciúme e o orgulho coexistem. Visualmente continua impressionante, a fotografia luminosa nunca contradiz a crescente sensação de inquietação, pelo contrário, parece intensificá-la, e também existe uma elegância quase hedonista na forma como Deray enquadra os corpos e os espaços, mas essa beleza nunca é gratuita, funciona como um contraste permanente com a deterioração psicológica das personagens. O meu interesse, e acho que o interesse geral, nunca esteve em descobrir o que vai acontecer, mas em observar como pequenas fissuras emocionais se transformam em algo irreversível. É um filme sofisticado e psicologicamente muito mais complexo do que eu pensei, mas gostei imenso.

A pesar de no ser para nada una película particularmente  ligera, con los años se ha consolidado como un comfort watch bien recurrente para mí. Mi segunda película favorita que involucra piscinas , sin duda. Yo se que está lejos de ser perfecta, porque definitivamente el componente de agobio y aislamiento que se va desarrollando, y que ante todo debería incomodarnos, hasta quizás chocarnos, termina quedándose más en la intención que un logro visual. Creo que Jacques Deray falla en contener tanto las emociones - en la cámara y en los personajes- y crea un ambiente tan fresco, tan pulcro y tan bello que termina contradiciendo esa parte fundamental del asunto. Es por eso que A bigger splash es una revisión tan interesante de esta y a la vez una gran película por sí misma, ahí  se convierte ese verano idílico en algo caótico e insoportable, se vuelve salvaje y también le dan más capas. Pero lo que es irresistible es todo el resto de la película. Para empezar es ver al star system Europeo de la época en todo su esplendor. Ese magnetismo y esa gracia y sin duda también ese atractivo no tiene punto de comparación. Alain Delon y Romy Schneider mejores que nunca, encima de todo tmb Jane Birkin. Los vestuarios son  inolvidables, la manera en que capturan el ocio y el hedonismo y el sol y las piscinas…. Nada mejor en vrd. Un caso muy claro de cómo una película puede fallar en sus objetivos pero estar filmada con tanto estilo y buen gusto que igual termine siendo inolvidable.
